transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-03-22
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Participants: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Nimbus ML), Tom Nguyen (Nimbus Infra), Sara O'Leary (Nimbus PM)

Summary section (auto):
- Quick recap: Nimbus saw a small but measurable drop in accuracy and a spike in tail latency after switching from fp16 to int8/GPTQ-ish pipeline in their VPC pilot. We walked through hypotheses: quantization algorithm mismatch (AWQ vs GPTQ), KV cache staleness / slot alignment, and batching causing tokenization boundary issues.

[00:00] Avery: okay everybody, thanks for carving out the time. quick check, audio okay?
[00:05] Maya: yep good here
[00:07] Tom: good
[00:09] Diego: audio's clear, i'll share my screen in a sec to show the repro traces
[00:18] Sara: just to set expectations, i'm mainly here for the pilot SLOs 
[00:21] Avery: perfect, we'll keep the SLO discussion toward the end, first we're going to go deep on the regression and reproduction.

[00:35] Diego: alright sharing now. so the root symptom you gave us was a ~2.2% drop in rouge/accuracy on your NLU tasks when you moved to int8 via the GPTQ workflow, and separately a p95 latency bump from ~140ms to ~210ms under your stage load. is that still accurate?
[00:50] Maya: yeah that's right. the accuracy drop is small but it fails some of our smoke tests. we also saw occasional tokens repeated in structured outputs which is weird.
[01:05] Tom: and in the VPC runs the variance is higher than our cloud tests, odd CPU steal maybe?

[01:20] Diego: okay. to be explicit, there are two quant paths we discussed: GPTQ-style per-layer calibration -> int8 kernels, and AWQ style grouped quant + per-channel scaling. they behave differently on biases and outlier tokens. AWQ often preserves certain head dynamics better but can introduce noise in softmax if scales aren't applied identically at serve time.
[01:46] Avery: we also saw that model conversion flags matter — e.g., whether the KV cache uses fp16 for keys/values vs quantized int8 for storage. that choice can change the generation path.

[02:05] Maya: can you explain the KV cache point? we thought K V cache was just storing previous keys and values, how would quantization change generations?
[02:15] Diego: good question. couple of things: first when you quantize the model weights but leave KV cache in fp16, you get a representation mismatch where the attention dot products are computed across mixed precisions. depending on kernel reorderings we sometimes see small numerical drifts that accumulate across long contexts — so repetition or odd probability shifts. second, some runtime optimizations pack KV cache into 8-bit buffers to save memory, and unpack lazily; that unpacking can shift alignment if the runtime uses cached offsets — we call that K V cash alignment issue in earlier docs, sorry for the mouthful.
[02:50] Tom: we did try enabling "kv quant" in one of our test runs to reduce memory, maybe that's related.

[03:05] Diego: yeah, that could be it. can i show the trace from your internal run?
[03:10] Maya: go ahead

[03:16] [screen share - perf traces]
[03:20] Diego: here's the request profile. note at step 0-3 token generation the sampling probs look fine, but around token 15 you see a drift in softmax distribution when the KV cache is used heavily. the inference log shows a switch to the int8 GEMM path at 12.8ms and then an fp16 fallback for certain residual ops. that fp16 fallback creates an extra GPU-sync which spikes p95.
[03:47] Maya: that matches what we saw — we saw the spike when context length increased.

[04:00] Avery: i want to call out a nuance: GPTQ conversions that aggressively per-layer quantize can make some attention matrices near-singular under certain inputs. AWQ's grouped approach can keep stability but sometimes at the cost of a slightly noisier distribution for tail tokens. so it's not always strictly better.
[04:22] Sara: so is there a clear rule — choose AWQ for better accuracy, GPTQ for speed?
[04:29] Diego: unfortunately, rule is workload dependent. for short-context Q&A where context is limited, GPTQ int8 often wins on throughput and retains quality. for long-form generation with 2k+ context, AWQ with fp16 KV or mixed-KV tends to preserve coherence better.
[04:48] Maya: our workload is a blend — chat summaries with ~1.2k average tokens, some 2k long reports. so it sits in the middle.
[04:58] Avery: then hybrid approach might be best: run AWQ for long-context routes and GPTQ-int8 for short ones, route by policy. Redwood's runtime can do per-route model variant routing so it's feasible.
[05:15] Tom: routing is fine but how do we keep unit economics? two variants sounds expensive.
[05:22] Avery: good point — that's where caching/prefix sharing helps. if you use trunked models with shared KV cache and smart routing the marginal cost per request can be small. we'll show a cost delta later.

[05:35] Diego: back to repro strategy. we propose three reproduction vectors: 1) deterministic tokenized input reproducer (seeded sampling, same tokenizer), 2) full VPC-run reproducer that mirrors their GPU flavor and runtime flags, 3) layerwise ablation where we quantize subsets of layers to find sensitivity.
[05:55] Maya: layer ablation sounds key — we suspected certain early-attention layers are sensitive.
[06:02] Diego: yeah often layer 0-3 or topmost residual block shows outsized impact. we can script a run that quantizes in blocks and reports delta-rouge.
[06:12] Avery: we also want to capture random seeds, tokenizers, temperature, top-k/top-p. tiny differences can look like regressions.
[06:22] Maya: we did pin temp and seed but will recheck.

[06:30] [07:00 marker noise / short pause]
[07:15] Tom: one other odd thing — our onprem racks show stagey CPU steal during bursts, could that explain the p95 delta?
[07:24] Diego: CPU steal on the host can increase host-to-device latency primarily for batch preparation and D2H copies. p50 maybe unaffected but p95 will jump. if you see correlation with host cpu spikes in the trace that may be a confounding factor.
[07:40] Maya: logs show small IO spikes during storage fetching of embeddings. we will capture iostat for the reproducer.

[07:50] Avery: operationally we recommend running the reproducer both with and without KV quant, with batch sizes 1 and 4, and with two different scheduling policies: on-demand and reserved. please include the exact kernel/version of the runtime.
[08:08] Diego: also turn on the runtime debug flag that logs kernel choices (int8_gemm_v2 vs fp16_gemm) and KV format. that helped us spot the lazy-unpack in earlier cases.

[08:25] Maya: quick aside — when you say "lazy-unpack" is it a runtime choice or conversion-time choice?
[08:32] Diego: it's runtime. conversion will produce a packed int8 representation, but some runtimes store packed bytes and only unpack to fp16 on-demand. if the unpack logic isn't atomic with the kernel it can cause alignment rounding differences.

[08:50] Sara: i want to understand the fallback strategy we mentioned earlier — if production sees regression on canary, what happens?
[08:58] Avery: our recommended flow: traffic split 5% canary using AWQ variant, monitor quality metrics (smoke evals) and latency SLOs for 24 hours; if regression > threshold (we can calibrate, e.g., >1% absolute rouge drop or >5% error on intents) then auto-fallback to fp16 variant and alert. we can configure automatic rollbacks.
[09:22] Tom: how fast is rollback? do sessions get lost?
[09:27] Diego: rollback is model-variant level; KV cache is model-variant specific so some sessions might see cold-starts; to minimize impact you can do sticky-routing for active sessions and degrade only new sessions. that keeps UX stable.
[09:40] Maya: hmm okay. we can accept slight cold-starts if accuracy is preserved.

[09:48] Diego: i also want to call out quantization math differences. AWQ uses grouped scales with a sgn-aware zero point approximation and sometimes uses stochastic rounding during conversion — that can change logits distribution subtly. GPTQ is more deterministic but can overcompress tail weights. both have tradeoffs.
[10:10] Avery: we had a case where AWQ converted had marginally better rouge on summarization but worse factuality because a few rare tokens shifted probability mass. it's subtle but real.

[10:28] Sara: so in terms of AB tests, what metric should we watch? ROUGE? BLEU? or something more product focused?
[10:35] Maya: we use a composite signal: ROUGE-L for high-level, plus our entity-extraction F1 for factuality. the smoke test flags on our side are entity F1 drop > 0.8%.
[10:46] Diego: include also hallucination checks and repetition rate. runtime can log token ngrams to detect repeats.

[10:56] [11:20] Diego: next let's talk about batching — we saw in your config you had batch_size 8 enabled for short tasks. batching can mask quantization noise because aggregated GEMMs increase numeric stability, but it raises latency for single-user interactions.
[11:40] Maya: we had batch_size 8 to save cost; but latency for interactive chat was painful.
[11:46] Avery: typical balanced approach: batch for bulk offline generation routes and keep interactive routes batch=1 with KV warm-up and micro-batching. Redwood has continuous batching which coalesces small requests with soft SLO bounds to improve throughput without spiking single-user tails.
[12:10] Tom: can you quantify throughput wins? we budgeted for 500 req/s across 8 GPUs.
[12:16] Diego: rough numbers from our internal bench: for this model family, fp16 batch=1 p50 ~45ms p95 ~130ms; int8 (GPTQ) batch=1 p50 ~38ms p95 ~150ms (p95 worse because of sync), int8 batch=8 throughput increases ~3.7x but p95 for interactive requests if not coalesced can jump to 400ms. AWQ mixed-KV batch=1 p50 ~42ms p95 ~140ms. these are ballpark and vary by GPU and kernel.
[12:52] Maya: interesting that int8 p50 is better but p95 worse.
[12:58] Diego: yeah that's the kernel-switching and unpack sync issue.

[13:10] Avery: on the VPC/onprem question: we've historically seen ±6-12% performance variation across customer hardware due to PCI-e layout, driver versions, and system-level interrupts. so when running the reproducer in your VPC please capture nvidia-smi, driver, and kernel versions.
[13:30] Tom: ours are Ampere A100 40GB with Ubuntu 22.04 and driver 545.x, CUDA 12 at the moment.
[13:38] Diego: perfect — please include the exact pcie gen and whether MIG is enabled if you use multi-tenant GPU.

[13:48] Maya: we also want to understand legality/compliance — will the runtime send logs out of VPC?
[13:54] Avery: for the Private pilot we run the control plane in a customer-managed VPC, logs stay in your account if you opt for that mode. Redwood hosted mode sends telemetry to Redwood but we can scrub PII. we'll share the SOC2 and KMS integration docs after this call.

[14:12] Sara: thanks.

[14:18] Diego: back to the triage plan. to narrow down layer sensitivity we'll do a 4-step bisect: quantize top half of layers only, bottom half only, then quadrant scanning (layers 0-3, 4-7, etc). collect delta-rouge and token-level KL to baseline fp16.
[14:36] Maya: KL sounds useful, we can set a threshold.

[14:42] Diego: and we will instrument token-probability tracking to spot shifting mass. if we see consistent negative KL in certain layers that points to local compression.

[14:56] Tom: how long will these experiments take?
[15:00] Diego: each layer-scan pass for your test set should take ~45 minutes on one GPU; parallelize across 4 GPUs to finish faster. the full ablation suite ~3-4 hours.

[15:12] Avery: for the pilot SLOs we propose: p50 latency < 60ms for interactive routes, p95 < 200ms, and entity F1 within 0.7% of fp16 baseline. fail the canary if both latency and quality breach thresholds.

[15:30] Sara: sounds reasonable, we'll review pricing with that in mind.

[15:36] Maya: one more thing — we noticed generation drift after warmup where early responses matched baseline then diverged after 100 requests. could that be KV cache staleness?
[15:46] Diego: yes, long-running processes that reuse quantized KV buffers without periodic normalization can accumulate error. we advise KV periodic re-normalization or occasional fp16 checkpointing. another technique is sticky-KV where hot sessions pin fp16 KV to avoid error accumulation.

[16:04] Tom: and what about determinism — are we going to see non-deterministic differences across runs?
[16:10] Diego: mixed precision can introduce non-determinism due to atomic reductions, nondeterministic kernels, and stochastic rounding. you can force deterministic kernels but performance may suffer. so practicality: use deterministic for regression testing, not for prod if you need max perf.

[16:28] Avery: okay let's capture agreed reproducible steps: 1) Diego to produce the repro bundle (AWQ, GPTQ conversions, conversion flags, seed inputs, perf logging flags). 2) Nimbus to run bundle in VPC with the provided runtime debug flags and upload logs. 3) joint 2-hour remote bench for bisect. 4) Redwood to draft pilot SLOs & fallback policy.

[16:56] Maya: agreed. Diego, what's in the repro bundle exactly?
[17:00] Diego: conversion scripts (python), a pinned tokenizer and seed corpus (1000 samples), a short eval harness that computes rouge/entity-f1/kl, runtime flag file with kernel toggles, and a sample workload driver to hit batch sizes 1/4/8. we'll put everything in a tarball and upload a link.
[17:20] Sara: will the repro include our production prompt templates?
[17:24] Maya: yes I'll include our top 30 templates.

[17:30] Diego: optionally we can give you a containerized runner so you don't need to install. but for VPC we prefer you run native so GPU access is direct.

[17:40] Tom: can we run the container with passthrough? we'll coordinate with infra.

[17:44] Avery: on the security docs, i'll send KMS integration steps and the SOC2 pack after.

[17:52] [18:00] Maya: minor note — when you say "probe layers 0-3" do you mean transformer blocks indexing from 0 or 1?
[18:00] Diego: from 0 (zero-indexed). we'll annotate in the script.

[18:10] Sara: ok great. anything else?
[18:14] Diego: one experimental idea — we can try stochastic mixed-precision where we randomly keep a subset of layers in fp16 during inference for 5-10% of requests to see if that helps tail quality without large cost.
[18:28] Maya: that's interesting, like a low-cost ensemble?
[18:32] Diego: yeah similar idea, you get diversity without full-cost. it's an ops trick not a formal algorithm.

[18:40] Avery: let's capture next meeting — proposed joint bench Tuesday 2028-03-28 at 09:00 PT, 2 hours. does that work?
[18:48] Sara: yes works for us
[18:50] Maya: works
[18:52] Tom: works

[18:56] Avery: great. final quick recap of deliverables: Diego will upload repro bundle by Friday, Avery will share SOC2/KMS docs and draft SLOs and pricing, Nimbus runs reproducer and shares logs, then joint bench next Tuesday.
[19:12] Maya: sounds good, thanks all
[19:15] Sara: thanks
[19:17] Diego: thanks everyone.

[19:20] Speaker 6: bye
